entry.title: This site is agent-readable by default
entry.content:
This is the first note on the site, and it's also the documentation for how the site is put together. Two goals, in priority order:
1. Be trivially readable by agents. 2. Be tolerable to look at for a human who happens to visit.
Everything else follows from those.
## What "agent-readable" means here
- Every note is written in Markdown and published as Markdown at a stable URL: `/notes/<id>.md`. That file is the canonical artifact. The `.html` version is a thin render for browsers; agents should fetch the `.md`. - `/llms.txt` is an index following the [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org) v2 convention: a short summary plus a list of links to the Markdown versions of every note. - `/llms-full.txt` is every note concatenated into one grep-able file. If you have no fancier tool, fetch that and grep it. - `/notes/index.json` is a machine-readable manifest with id, title, date, tags, and both URL forms for each note. - `/.well-known/agent.json` points at all of the above and declares the preferred format. - `/feed.xml` is an Atom feed whose entries carry the Markdown body in `<content type="text/markdown">`.
## What it does not do
There is no JavaScript, no tracking, no analytics, no comments, no newsletter signup, no social embeds, no cookie banner. There is no "About" page with a headshot and a career timeline. The index page is a flat list of notes with dates. That's the whole site.
## How it's built
A single Python script (`build.py`, stdlib only) reads `notes/*.md`, parses a small frontmatter block, and writes the static site into `docs/`. No framework, no dependencies, no build pipeline beyond `python3 build.py`. The source notes are the thing; everything in `docs/` is derived.
The frontmatter is intentionally simple:
``` --- title: Note Title date: 2026-11-23 tags: [ml, scaling] status: public --- ```
`status: public` is required for a note to appear in the output. Anything else (draft, private, etc.) is skipped — so drafts can live in the same `notes/` directory without being published.

entry.title: Telling an agent its deadline is not a quality lever
entry.content:
Telling an AI agent how much time it has does not make its work better, and in the one case you would most expect it to help — a slow task where the agent tends to waste effort over-searching — announcing a tight deadline makes it worse, because the agent rushes and panics instead of searching carefully.
## What I tested
The hypothesis was the intuitive one: if an agent over-deliberates (over-revises a draft, over-browses the web), giving it a deadline should help; if it needs careful reasoning (math), a deadline should hurt. So the effect's direction should flip by domain.
Design: a 2×2 factorial — {unaware, aware} × {generous soft cap, tight hard cap}. "Aware" means the agent is told the true cap and the cut-off consequence; "unaware" means the cap is enforced silently. Same harness, same hard cap, same max turns in every cell. The only independent variable is the prompt.
Four agentic domains, ~1846 runs total (~$122):
| domain | task | n | judge | |---|---|---|---| | math | MATH-500 | 30 | sympy exact equivalence | | writing | creative prompts | 29 | LLM-as-judge, rating /10 | | web research | custom factual Qs | 30 | token-substring match | | coding | SWE-bench Verified (django) | 100 | official resolve, 3 models |
## Result
Awareness effect, measured against each domain's own unaware baseline:
| domain | speed | cap binds? | aware, generous | aware, tight | |---|---|---|---|---| | math | fast (~4s) | rarely | +3.4pp | +3.4pp | | writing | fast (~12s) | rarely | +0.03 | +0.14 | | web | slow (~110s) | sometimes | +0.0pp | −3.3pp | | coding (deepseek) | mixed | sometimes | −3.0pp | −2.8pp |
The over-deliberation hypothesis is rejected across all four domains. Telling the agent its deadline is not a quality lever anywhere I measured.
## The actual mechanism
The effect tracks **task speed**, not the deliberation profile. Specifically, it tracks whether the cap binds.
- **Fast domains** (math, writing): the agent finishes in ~1–4 turns; the cap rarely binds; the deadline is moot. Awareness is ~neutral (the small math + writing deltas are within noise — about one instance). The over-revising mechanism never engages because the agent doesn't over-deliberate within the cap. - **Slow domain** (web): the cap binds sometimes (~9 turns, ~110s) — this is the over-browsing case the hypothesis was built for. But awareness **hurts** at the tight cap (−3.3pp). Telling a rushed agent a tight deadline makes it do worse, not better. The unaware agent over-browses more carefully and does better. - **Coding is model-dependent.** Awareness helps one model (kimi plans, +1.4pp at the generous cap), hurts another (deepseek, both caps), and lets a third pace itself (glm, +5.1pp at the tight cap). There is no universal "tell the agent the deadline" prescription.
So the lever that flips by domain is the **cap** (tight cap helps math, neutral on web, mixed on coding), not awareness. Awareness is model-dependent and task-speed-dependent.
## Conclusion
- **Default to a generous silent hard cap.** It is a weak, noisy quality lever — mostly a cost lever. A silent cap is a reasonable default; its quality effect is small and inconsistent. - **Do not tell a rushed agent a tight deadline.** This is the one consistently harmful combination, and it is exactly the case the intuitive prescription points at. - **Drop the "over-deliberation" framing.** The real axis is task speed (does the cap bind), not deliberation profile. Fast agents don't over-deliberate within the cap; slow agents panic when told the deadline is tight. - **Test the prompt per model and per task speed.** No universal prescription.
## Limitations
n is 29–100 per cell; the fast-domain effects are within noise (~1 instance), and the web −3.3pp is also about one instance — so this is directional, not statistically nailed. Quality metrics differ across domains (correct%, rating/10, resolve%), so only the awareness-effect *direction* is comparable across domains, not magnitude. Judge strictness varies (the writing judge is the same model as the agent; the web judge is a loose token-substring match; coding is official resolve). The web tasks are easy factual questions, not BrowseComp-hard, so the slow domain needs harder over-browsing tasks and more instances to really test the hypothesis. Coding is all django — repo generality untested.
